CURRENT AFFAIRS 210
Greater BRICS Economic Cooperation: AI Open-Source Zone, SEZ
Partnership and Services Trade
Category GS Date Quick rule
International Relations, Economy GS II / GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• At the New Delhi BRICS summit, China proposed a BRICS AI Open-Source Zone, a Special Economic Zone partnership and a services-trade
forum. The New Delhi meeting is the 18th BRICS Summit, held on 12-13 September 2026.
• The proposals seek denser economic links across an expanded BRICS while preserving national policy space.
• For India, the opportunity lies in standards, digital public infrastructure, services exports and diversified supply chains.
WHY IN NEWS
• The 13 September summit session shifted attention from BRICS political messaging to practical economic platforms. BRICS now has 10
full members: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE and Indonesia.
• The debate matters because expansion has increased BRICS weight but also made consensus and implementation harder.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• The New Delhi meeting is the 18th BRICS Summit, held on 12-13 September 2026.
• BRICS now has 10 full members: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE and Indonesia.
• The original BRIC leaders held their first summit in 2009; South Africa joined in 2010.
• The New Development Bank was established in 2015 with authorised capital of US$100 billion.
• BRICS economies together account for more than 40% of the world population.
• China is due to chair BRICS and host the 19th summit in 2027.
• BRICS began as BRIC and became BRICS after South Africa joined in 2010.
• The grouping expanded significantly from 2024 onward and now includes major economies from Asia, Africa, Latin America and West Asia.
• India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi in September 2026.
• China proposed a BRICS AI Open-Source Zone.
• China also proposed cooperation among BRICS Special Economic Zones.
• A BRICS services-trade forum was proposed for China.
• Supply-chain resilience was a major theme at the summit.
• BRICS is not a customs union, common market or military alliance.
• Decisions are generally consensus-based and non-treaty in character.
• The New Development Bank is the grouping’s principal multilateral financial institution.
• India supports reform of global governance while retaining strategic autonomy.
• Practical cooperation must manage differences in regulation, data governance, sanctions exposure and market access.

Greater BRICS Economic Cooperation: AI Open-Source Zone, SEZ

Category GS Date Quick rule

PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
Can an expanded BRICS become a platform for practical economic cooperation without evolving into a rigid geopolitical bloc? Discuss
from India’s perspective.
MODEL ANSWER (~300 WORDS)
INTRODUCTION
The New Delhi meeting is the 18th BRICS Summit, held on 12-13 September 2026. BRICS now has 10 full members: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa,
Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE and Indonesia. The original BRIC leaders held their first summit in 2009; South Africa joined in 2010. Common digital standards can
lower transaction costs without requiring a single regulatory regime.
SIGNIFICANCE
• The original BRIC leaders held their first summit in 2009; South Africa joined in 2010. Common digital standards can lower transaction costs without
requiring a single regulatory regime.
• The New Development Bank was established in 2015 with authorised capital of US$100 billion. SEZ-to-SEZ cooperation may connect industrial clusters,
logistics networks and investment pipelines.
• Services trade and open-source AI can widen participation by smaller developing economies.
• India can use BRICS to internationalise interoperable digital public infrastructure while avoiding technological dependence.
• The numerical context is important: BRICS economies together account for more than 40% of the world population.
• Institutional context also matters: China is due to chair BRICS and host the 19th summit in 2027.
CHALLENGES
• Membership diversity makes common standards difficult.
• Sanctions and geopolitical disputes can complicate finance and technology cooperation.
• China’s economic weight may create asymmetry.
• Announcements need measurable projects, financing and dispute-management mechanisms.
WAY FORWARD
• Set up interoperable but voluntary technical standards for AI, services and SEZ cooperation rather than a single rigid BRICS rulebook.
• Use the New Development Bank and national development institutions to finance demonstrable cross-border projects with transparent procurement.
• India should push open digital standards that protect data sovereignty while enabling Indian firms and public digital infrastructure to scale across BRICS
markets.
• Create annual implementation scorecards covering services trade, investment, SEZ links and technology projects so summit announcements can be
measured.
CONCLUSION
For India, a larger BRICS is useful only if flexible cooperation produces finance, trade and technology outcomes without eroding strategic autonomy.

CURRENT AFFAIRS 211
BRICS Agriculture Platforms: AGRIN, Agroecology, Digital Agriculture
and Farmers’ Rights
Category GS Date Quick rule
Agriculture, International Relations GS II / GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• Four agriculture platforms were highlighted at the BRICS summit, including AGRIN and networks on agroecology and digital agriculture. The
agriculture package was highlighted during the 18th BRICS Summit of 12-13 September 2026.
• A Global Forum on Farmers’ Rights in Seed Systems seeks cooperation on seeds, genetic resources and traditional knowledge.
• The initiatives connect climate resilience, productivity, biodiversity and fair agricultural trade.
WHY IN NEWS
• The summit operationalised outcomes of the 2026 BRICS Agriculture Ministers’ process rather than limiting cooperation to declarations.
The package contains 4 highlighted cooperation platforms: AGRIN, agroecology/regenerative agriculture, digital agriculture and a
farmers-rights seed forum.
• India has an interest in farmer-centric technology sharing that protects genetic resources and policy space.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• The agriculture package was highlighted during the 18th BRICS Summit of 12-13 September 2026.
• The package contains 4 highlighted cooperation platforms: AGRIN, agroecology/regenerative agriculture, digital agriculture and a farmers-rights seed forum.
• BRICS has 10 full members in 2026, widening the potential agricultural knowledge network.
• South Africa joined the original BRIC grouping in 2010.
• The 2026 BRICS agriculture process included a ministerial meeting in Indore before the leaders summit.
• The WTO Agreement on Agriculture has 3 principal pillars: market access, domestic support and export competition.
• India's Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act dates to 2001.
• The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture entered into force in 2004.
• India is a contracting party to the ITPGRFA.
• Farmers' Rights concern seed, traditional knowledge, benefit sharing and participation.
• Agroecology integrates ecological principles into farming systems.
• Regenerative agriculture focuses on soil function, biodiversity and resource cycles.
• Digital agriculture includes remote sensing, advisory services, farm data and decision tools.
• Seed-system cooperation can support climate-resilient varieties.
• Genetic-resource exchange raises access-and-benefit-sharing questions.
• Smallholders need affordable technology and extension support.
• BRICS agriculture cooperation can complement, not replace, FAO and other global mechanisms.
• India must balance innovation, biodiversity conservation and farmers’ seed rights.

• Joint platforms can help developing countries shape food-system standards.
• The numerical context is important: The 2026 BRICS agriculture process included a ministerial meeting in Indore before the leaders summit.

CURRENT AFFAIRS 212
BRICS Infectious-Disease Early Warning System: Health Security as
Global Public Infrastructure
Category GS Date Quick rule
Health, International Relations GS II / GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• BRICS leaders backed an infectious-disease early-warning system and stronger health cooperation. The proposal was highlighted at the 18th
BRICS Summit held on 12-13 September 2026.
• Cross-border outbreaks require surveillance, laboratory data and rapid risk communication before hospital systems are overwhelmed.
• India can contribute digital public-health infrastructure, pharmaceutical capacity and disease-surveillance experience.
WHY IN NEWS
• Pandemic experience shifted health security from a domestic welfare issue to a core element of economic and national resilience. BRICS
now has 10 full members, giving the proposed alert system a wide geographic footprint.
• The challenge is to build interoperability without creating a rival or fragmented international health architecture.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• The proposal was highlighted at the 18th BRICS Summit held on 12-13 September 2026.
• BRICS now has 10 full members, giving the proposed alert system a wide geographic footprint.
• The WHO International Health Regulations were adopted in 2005 and entered into force in 2007.
• The IHR framework covers 196 States Parties.
• WHO declared COVID-19 a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 30 January 2020.
• WHO characterised COVID-19 as a pandemic on 11 March 2020.
• WHO ended the COVID-19 PHEIC on 5 May 2023.
• India created the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme in 2004.
• The IHR 2005 is the principal international legal framework for cross-border public-health events.
• Early warning requires both event-based and indicator-based surveillance.
• Laboratories are needed to confirm suspected outbreaks.
• Genomic surveillance can identify variants and transmission patterns.
• Cross-border data exchange must protect privacy and national security.
• Risk communication is part of outbreak response.
• Health emergencies can disrupt trade, mobility, education and supply chains.
• India has major vaccine and generic-pharmaceutical production capacity.
• The National Centre for Disease Control is a key Indian public-health institution.
• A BRICS system should complement WHO rather than create incompatible reporting channels.

MODEL ANSWER (~300 WORDS)
INTRODUCTION
The proposal was highlighted at the 18th BRICS Summit held on 12-13 September 2026. BRICS now has 10 full members, giving the proposed alert system a
wide geographic footprint. The IHR 2005 is the principal international legal framework for cross-border public-health events. Faster detection reduces the
time between spillover and intervention.
SIGNIFICANCE
• The IHR 2005 is the principal international legal framework for cross-border public-health events. Faster detection reduces the time between spillover and
intervention.
• Early warning requires both event-based and indicator-based surveillance. Shared laboratory and genomic data can improve outbreak characterisation.
• India can contribute vaccine, pharmaceutical and digital-health capabilities.
• South-South cooperation can reduce dependence on a few global suppliers during emergencies.
• The numerical context is important: WHO declared COVID-19 a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 30 January 2020.
• Institutional context also matters: WHO characterised COVID-19 as a pandemic on 11 March 2020.
CHALLENGES
• States may delay reporting because of economic or reputational costs.
• Data standards may be incompatible.
• Sensitive health data raises privacy concerns.
• Parallel institutions can fragment global governance.
WAY FORWARD
• Develop common outbreak-alert protocols that can exchange minimum essential data rapidly while respecting national privacy and sovereignty rules.
• Align BRICS surveillance cooperation with WHO International Health Regulations to avoid fragmented global health architecture.
• Invest in laboratories, genomic surveillance and field epidemiology so early-warning systems are backed by domestic detection capacity.
• Run periodic multi-country simulation exercises and publish response-time indicators to test whether alerts lead to faster containment.
CONCLUSION
A BRICS early-warning network can add value when faster detection is connected to laboratories, trusted data exchange and the wider global health system.

articles.title: India’s High September Power Demand: Heat, Rainfall Deficit and Energy-System Stress
articles.fullText:
CURRENT AFFAIRS 213
India’s High September Power Demand: Heat, Rainfall Deficit and
Energy-System Stress
Category GS Date Quick rule
Economy, Environment GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• India’s electricity demand rose unusually strongly in September as heat and weaker rainfall increased cooling and irrigation loads. India's all-time
peak power demand crossed 250 GW in 2024, showing the scale of the grid that must absorb weather-driven spikes.
• The episode illustrates how climate variability increasingly affects electricity planning and fuel demand.
• Grid resilience now depends on forecasting, flexible generation, storage, transmission and demand response.
WHY IN NEWS
• Electricity demand is becoming more weather-sensitive as incomes, air-conditioning and irrigation loads rise. India crossed 200 GW of
peak demand for the first time in 2022 and exceeded 250 GW in 2024.
• A high-demand September can stress coal inventories, gas availability and evening balancing.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• India's all-time peak power demand crossed 250 GW in 2024, showing the scale of the grid that must absorb weather-driven spikes.
• India crossed 200 GW of peak demand for the first time in 2022 and exceeded 250 GW in 2024.
• September 2026 is part of the southwest monsoon season, which normally spans June to September.
• A 1°C increase in temperature can materially raise cooling load in large urban systems.
• Solar generation is strongest in daytime, while India's system peak often occurs in evening hours.
• Coal remains the largest source of electricity generation in India, so demand spikes can raise thermal dispatch and fuel burn.
• Pumped storage and batteries can shift energy across hours rather than create primary energy.
• Electricity demand is highly weather-sensitive.
• Cooling demand rises during hot and humid conditions.
• Weak rainfall can raise agricultural pumping in irrigated regions.
• Hydropower availability depends on reservoir inflows.
• Solar generation peaks during daylight while evening demand may remain high.
• Coal remains India’s largest electricity-generation source.
• Gas can provide flexibility but fuel cost matters.
• Battery storage can shift electricity across hours.
• Demand response can reduce peak stress without adding generation.
• Transmission constraints can create regional shortages even when national capacity is adequate.
• Climate adaptation and power-system planning are increasingly connected.

India’s High September Power Demand: Heat, Rainfall Deficit and
Energy-System Stress
Category GS Date Quick rule
Economy, Environment GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
Weather volatility is becoming a structural challenge for India’s electricity system. Discuss the implications and the role of flexibility, storage
and demand management.
MODEL ANSWER (~300 WORDS)
INTRODUCTION
India's all-time peak power demand crossed 250 GW in 2024, showing the scale of the grid that must absorb weather-driven spikes. India crossed 200 GW of
peak demand for the first time in 2022 and exceeded 250 GW in 2024. Cooling and irrigation can create simultaneous weather-driven demand shocks. Better
forecasting can reduce emergency procurement and reserve stress.
SIGNIFICANCE
• Cooling and irrigation can create simultaneous weather-driven demand shocks. Better forecasting can reduce emergency procurement and reserve stress.
• Electricity demand is highly weather-sensitive. Storage can bridge part of the solar-evening mismatch.
• Demand response can reduce peak load more cheaply than permanent over-capacity in some situations.
• Grid planning must incorporate climate scenarios.
• The numerical context is important: Solar generation is strongest in daytime, while India's system peak often occurs in evening hours.
• Institutional context also matters: Coal remains the largest source of electricity generation in India, so demand spikes can raise thermal dispatch and fuel burn.
CHALLENGES
• Extreme weather is hard to forecast precisely.
• Storage remains capital-intensive.
• Distribution companies have weak demand-response capability.
• Coal and gas flexibility have cost and emissions consequences.
WAY FORWARD
• Strengthen short-term load forecasting by integrating temperature, rainfall, humidity and renewable-generation data into dispatch decisions.
• Expand storage, flexible generation and demand-response programmes so peak demand does not translate automatically into fossil-fuel stress.
• Use time-of-day tariffs and industrial demand management to reduce expensive evening peaks without compromising productive activity.
• Accelerate transmission upgrades and energy-efficiency measures because reliability depends on both adequate capacity and lower peak intensity.
CONCLUSION
Peak electricity demand is ultimately a systems problem: India needs better forecasting, flexible capacity and efficiency as much as additional generation.

CURRENT AFFAIRS 214
RBI Liquidity Management: Bond Sales, FX Swaps and Monetary-Policy
Transmission
Category GS Date Quick rule
Economy GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• RBI liquidity operations use several instruments, including repos, reverse repos, bond transactions and foreign-exchange swaps. India's inflation-
targeting framework formally centres on a 4% CPI target with a +/-2 percentage-point tolerance band.
• Liquidity conditions influence the transmission of the policy rate to overnight and broader money-market rates.
• FX operations can affect both the exchange rate and rupee liquidity, requiring coordination across policy objectives.
WHY IN NEWS
• Attention has turned to the RBI’s mix of liquidity absorption and injection as financial conditions shift. The RBI's liquidity toolkit spans
maturities from overnight facilities to longer-tenor variable-rate operations and government-security transactions.
• The issue is distinct from a change in the monetary-policy stance itself.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• India's inflation-targeting framework formally centres on a 4% CPI target with a +/-2 percentage-point tolerance band.
• The RBI's liquidity toolkit spans maturities from overnight facilities to longer-tenor variable-rate operations and government-security transactions.
• The Monetary Policy Committee has 6 members under the RBI Act framework.
• MPC decisions are taken by majority, with the RBI Governor holding a casting vote in the event of a tie.
• The Liquidity Adjustment Facility is built around short-term liquidity management.
• Open-market operations involve outright purchase or sale of government securities.
• The Standing Deposit Facility was introduced in 2022.
• RBI adopted inflation targeting in its current statutory framework in 2016.
• A repo injects liquidity against eligible collateral.
• A reverse repo or deposit facility absorbs liquidity.
• Open-market purchases inject durable liquidity.
• Open-market sales absorb durable liquidity.
• An FX swap exchanges currencies for specified maturities.
• RBI dollar purchases can inject rupee liquidity unless sterilised.
• RBI dollar sales can absorb rupee liquidity unless offset.
• Money-market rates transmit the policy stance to broader credit conditions.
• Durable and frictional liquidity are different concepts.
• Liquidity tools should not be confused automatically with policy-rate changes.

Explain why central-bank liquidity management matters for monetary-policy transmission. How do bond operations and foreign-exchange
swaps interact with domestic liquidity?
MODEL ANSWER (~300 WORDS)
INTRODUCTION
India's inflation-targeting framework formally centres on a 4% CPI target with a +/-2 percentage-point tolerance band. The RBI's liquidity toolkit spans maturities
from overnight facilities to longer-tenor variable-rate operations and government-security transactions. A repo injects liquidity against eligible collateral.
Adequate liquidity keeps overnight rates close to the policy target.
SIGNIFICANCE
• A repo injects liquidity against eligible collateral. Adequate liquidity keeps overnight rates close to the policy target.
• A reverse repo or deposit facility absorbs liquidity. OMOs influence durable system liquidity.
• FX swaps can manage external and domestic liquidity simultaneously.
• Transmission becomes weaker when money-market rates diverge persistently from the policy stance.
• The numerical context is important: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility is built around short-term liquidity management.
• Institutional context also matters: Open-market operations involve outright purchase or sale of government securities.
CHALLENGES
• Large capital flows can create volatile liquidity.
• FX and inflation objectives can conflict.
• Durable liquidity estimates are uncertain.
• Market expectations can over-interpret routine operations.
WAY FORWARD
• RBI should distinguish durable liquidity deficits from temporary friction before choosing between bond operations, variable-rate repos and FX swaps.
• Communicate the expected liquidity effect and maturity profile of operations so markets can separate monetary-policy stance from liquidity management.
• Deepen collateral and government-securities markets to improve transmission from the policy rate to money-market and lending rates.
• Coordinate liquidity operations with foreign-exchange management carefully so intervention does not unintentionally offset the intended monetary signal.
CONCLUSION
Liquidity management works best when markets understand both the policy-rate signal and the temporary instruments used to keep short-term rates aligned with it.

• RBI’s scale-based framework classifies NBFCs by size, activity and systemic risk, with stronger rules for the upper layer. RBI introduced the Scale Based
Regulation framework for NBFCs in October 2021.
• Tata Sons’ listing question highlights how a private holding company can become systemically important through financial structure.
• The case raises questions of proportional regulation, corporate restructuring and market transparency.
WHY IN NEWS
• RBI reportedly rejected a request by Tata Sons to avoid a public listing under the upper-layer framework. The framework broadly uses 4
regulatory layers: Base, Middle, Upper and a possible Top Layer.
• The issue is about regulatory status and systemic risk, not simply a voluntary IPO decision.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• RBI introduced the Scale Based Regulation framework for NBFCs in October 2021.
• The framework broadly uses 4 regulatory layers: Base, Middle, Upper and a possible Top Layer.
• Upper Layer entities face enhanced prudential and governance requirements.
• The framework became effective in stages from 2022.
• RBI identifies Upper Layer NBFCs using parameters that include size, leverage, interconnectedness and supervisory inputs.
• Public listing is one of the important governance requirements associated with specified Upper Layer entities.
• NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits like banks.
• NBFC regulation is primarily under the RBI Act, 1934.
• RBI's SBR framework has four layers.
• NBFC-Upper Layer entities face enhanced prudential regulation.
• RBI can identify systemically important entities based on size, activity and risk.
• Listing can increase public disclosure and market scrutiny.
• Tata Sons is the principal holding company of the Tata group.
• A holding company may be systemically relevant even without conventional retail banking.
• RBI supervision and corporate-law requirements can overlap.
• Restructuring to avoid regulatory classification raises moral-hazard concerns.
• Proportional regulation seeks to match compliance with risk.
• Financial conglomerates create interconnectedness risk.

INTRODUCTION
RBI introduced the Scale Based Regulation framework for NBFCs in October 2021. The framework broadly uses 4 regulatory layers: Base, Middle, Upper and a
possible Top Layer. RBI's SBR framework has four layers. A risk-based structure targets supervision where failure could have wider consequences.
SIGNIFICANCE
• RBI's SBR framework has four layers. A risk-based structure targets supervision where failure could have wider consequences.
• NBFC-Upper Layer entities face enhanced prudential regulation. Listing can improve disclosure, valuation and external scrutiny.
• Governance requirements can reduce opaque related-party and group risks.
• The framework reduces the regulatory gap between very large NBFCs and banks without making them identical.
• The numerical context is important: RBI identifies Upper Layer NBFCs using parameters that include size, leverage, interconnectedness and supervisory inputs.
• Institutional context also matters: Public listing is one of the important governance requirements associated with specified Upper Layer entities.
CHALLENGES
• Listing may conflict with promoter preferences.
• Group restructuring can shift risk without reducing it.
• Market listing is not a substitute for supervision.
• One-size-fits-all timelines can be disruptive.
WAY FORWARD
• Apply Scale-Based Regulation through clear, predictable compliance timelines so large NBFCs cannot defer obligations through repeated restructuring.
• Require governance, related-party and risk disclosures proportionate to systemic importance before any public listing or major corporate reorganisation.
• RBI should preserve case-by-case supervisory flexibility while publishing enough reasoning to reduce uncertainty for similarly placed upper-layer NBFCs.
• Any transition should protect financial stability and minority investors rather than treating listing as a purely procedural corporate-law event.
CONCLUSION
Scale-Based Regulation is credible when systemically important NBFCs face predictable governance and disclosure obligations comparable to the risks they create.

SEBI Cyber-Security Framework for Market-Infrastructure Subsidiaries
Category GS Date Quick rule
Economy, Cyber Security GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• SEBI proposed a proportional cyber-security framework for subsidiaries of market infrastructure institutions. SEBI issued its Cybersecurity and Cyber
Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for regulated entities on 20 August 2024.
• The objective is to prevent weaker subsidiary controls from becoming attack paths into exchanges, clearing corporations or depositories.
• Risk classification and group-level governance are more useful than treating every subsidiary identically.
WHY IN NEWS
• Market infrastructure is increasingly interconnected through shared networks, vendors and data. SEBI issued clarifications to the CSCRF on 31
December 2024 and a further implementation extension on 28 March 2025.
• Cyber resilience is now a financial-stability concern rather than a back-office IT issue.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• SEBI issued its Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for regulated entities on 20 August 2024.
• SEBI issued clarifications to the CSCRF on 31 December 2024 and a further implementation extension on 28 March 2025.
• SEBI received statutory status under the SEBI Act, 1992.
• The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act dates to 1956 and the Depositories Act to 1996.
• India has 2 national securities depositories: NSDL and CDSL.
• India completed the market-wide shift to T+1 rolling settlement for listed equities in 2023.
• T+1 means settlement normally occurs 1 business day after the trade date.
• Cyber incidents measured in minutes can disrupt millions of electronic orders, so recovery-time and recovery-point objectives are operationally significant.
• The securities-market infrastructure can be grouped into 3 core MII functions: trading, clearing and depository services.
• The core stock-market infrastructure includes exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories operating on near-continuous electronic systems.
• SEBI was given statutory status in 1992.
• India moved to T+1 rolling settlement for the equity cash market in 2023.
• A useful cyber-resilience cycle has 4 operational stages: prevention, detection, response and recovery.
• The framework extends cyber-governance expectations to subsidiaries because a single weak link can compromise a larger market-infrastructure group.
• MIIs include stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories.
• Clearing corporations manage counterparty and settlement risk.
• Depositories hold securities in dematerialised form.
• Cyber resilience includes prevention, detection, response and recovery.

SEBI Cyber-Security Framework for Market-Infrastructure Subsidiaries
Category GS Date Quick rule
Economy, Cyber Security GS III 13 Sep 2026 Read highlighted facts first
PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
Why must cyber-security regulation extend beyond core exchanges to subsidiaries and service providers in market-infrastructure groups?
MODEL ANSWER (~300 WORDS)
INTRODUCTION
SEBI issued its Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for regulated entities on 20 August 2024. SEBI issued clarifications to the CSCRF on 31
December 2024 and a further implementation extension on 28 March 2025. SEBI was given statutory status in 1992. Attackers target the weakest connected
component rather than the most regulated entity.
SIGNIFICANCE
• SEBI was given statutory status in 1992. Attackers target the weakest connected component rather than the most regulated entity.
• India moved to T+1 rolling settlement for the equity cash market in 2023. Common minimum controls can reduce regulatory arbitrage.
• Criticality mapping allows stronger controls for subsidiaries that handle sensitive data or core operations.
• Sector-wide drills can test recovery dependencies across institutions.
• The numerical context is important: India has 2 national securities depositories: NSDL and CDSL.
• Institutional context also matters: India completed the market-wide shift to T+1 rolling settlement for listed equities in 2023.
CHALLENGES
• Overbroad rules can impose high costs on low-risk entities.
• Legacy systems and outsourcing complicate visibility.
• Cyber metrics can become compliance checklists rather than resilience measures.
• Incident disclosure must balance transparency with security.
WAY FORWARD
• Require every market-infrastructure group to maintain a current asset map covering subsidiaries, vendors, privileged access and critical data flows.
• Mandate realistic cyber-recovery drills across exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories, including failure of a key third-party service provider.
• Use risk-based controls so low-risk subsidiaries are not overburdened while entities connected to trading, clearing or settlement face stricter requirements.
• Improve incident reporting and sector-wide threat intelligence so a vulnerability discovered in one institution can be contained across the market quickly.
CONCLUSION
Cyber resilience in securities markets depends on the weakest connected entity; group-wide testing and recovery therefore matter as much as perimeter
security.

• The case concerns social-security gaps in private schools against statutory reference points including the 1952 EPF Act, 1948 ESI Act and 1972
gratuity law.
• The issue sits at the intersection of education regulation, labour welfare and federalism.
• A policy challenge is to protect teachers without destabilising low-fee schools or duplicating existing labour laws.
WHY IN NEWS
• Private-school teachers often fall under fragmented state rules and employment arrangements. The Employees' Provident Funds law
generally applies to covered establishments with 20 or more employees, subject to statutory conditions.
• The Court sought responses from the Union, States, UTs and education authorities.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years.
• The Right to Education Act was enacted in 2009 and came into force on 1 April 2010.

• The Payment of Gratuity Act dates to 1972.

• India has more than 1 million schools across government and private management categories.
• The Employees' Provident Funds law generally applies to covered establishments with 20 or more employees, subject to statutory conditions.
• The ESI framework generally covers notified establishments and eligible wage categories, with thresholds prescribed by law.
• The Supreme Court notice in 2026 concerns welfare protection for a workforce spread across thousands of private schools.
• India has more than 1 million schools across government and private management categories, showing the scale of the education workforce.
• Education is in the Concurrent List.

INTRODUCTION
Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years. The Right to Education Act was enacted in 2009 and came into force on 1
April 2010. The ESI framework generally covers notified establishments and eligible wage categories, with thresholds prescribed by law. Teacher welfare
supports professional stability and educational quality.
SIGNIFICANCE
• The ESI framework generally covers notified establishments and eligible wage categories, with thresholds prescribed by law. Teacher welfare supports
professional stability and educational quality.
• The Supreme Court notice in 2026 concerns welfare protection for a workforce spread across thousands of private schools. A national floor can reduce
arbitrary variation while allowing states to add protection.
• Digital payroll records can improve compliance and portability.
• Targeted support may be needed for genuinely low-fee schools serving disadvantaged communities.
• The numerical context is important: The Payment of Gratuity Act dates to 1972.
• Institutional context also matters: The EPF law generally applies to covered establishments with 20 or more employees, subject to statutory conditions.
CHALLENGES
• School finances vary sharply across regions.
• Informal contracts make enforcement difficult.
• Overlapping central and state rules can create confusion.
• Uniform mandates can unintentionally raise fees or encourage evasion.
WAY FORWARD
• Create a statutory minimum social-security floor for private-school teachers covering provident-fund, insurance and retirement protection where existing
schemes do not apply.
• Clarify the division of responsibility among school managements, states and the Union so contribution obligations cannot be shifted indefinitely.
• Build grievance and inspection systems that protect teachers from retaliation while allowing financially weak schools proportionate compliance pathways.
• Any reform should preserve educational affordability while recognising that long-term teacher insecurity can also damage retention and learning quality.
CONCLUSION
Extending social protection to private-school teachers can strengthen both labour dignity and educational quality if financing and compliance are designed
proportionately.
